newsitem.title: USA: Pitfalls seen in revamping Florida telecom taxes.
newsitem.headline: Pitfalls seen in revamping Florida telecom taxes.

text.p: State lawmakers revamping Florida's telecommunications tax code may meet more resistance from local municipal governments than from the industries whose services will be taxed, the head of a state task force said Thursday.

Alan Johansen is policy coordinator for the Florida governor's Office of Planning and Budgeting and also chairs the 19-member task force charged with advising the legislature on how to adapt the tax structure to reflect the easing of barriers that have historically separated the cable television and local and long-distance telephone services.

Florida's telecommunications taxes currently bring in $1 billion annually, through a hodgedpodge of sales taxes, gross receipts taxes, public service taxes and franchise taxes. Each in turn has a complicated rate schedule that differentiates between residential and commercial services, and various types of services.
"They all apply to different places at different rates," Johansen said.

The rate structure has been rendered obsolete under state legislative changes and the federal Telecommunications Act of 1996, which paved the way for telephone, audio, cable and internet services to be delivered by a single provider, Johansen said.
"You are really going to lose the ability to distinguish," Johansen said.

In a move he described as "really quite astounding," the Florida Telecommunications Industry Association, which includes both small companies and the major industry players, have proposed one unified, statewide telecommunications levy that would tax all telecommunications services at a flat rate of about 9 percent to 10 percent.
"There will be some winners and losers," under the plan, Johansen said. But the companies resisted urge to gouge any one sector because they may soon enter that sector, he said.
"They are all getting into each other's industries," he said.
But it will not be as easy to draft the distribution formula for dividing those shared revenues to local governments because some of the taxes are currently local option taxes, Johansen said.
Under a unified formula, consumers in counties that have not previously levied the taxes would have to start paying them.

Those counties would in turn demand a share of the revenue and would likely balk if they received back less money per capita than other municipalities. At the same time, those that currently collect the taxes locally would have to rely on state collections and distributions.

"It's a very significant source of funding," he said. "It's a very sensitive issue for cities and counties. The issue is whether you can take their tax away, impose it at the state level and then (give) it back."

At the same time, about half of the current revenues, or $500 million a year, are pledged to debt service on bonds, including Florida Board of Education issues. Lawmakers cannot reduce those revenues without illegally impairing contractual obligations to bondholders.
"The state is very sensitive in this area and will take no action that will impair these revenues," Johansen said.
His task force is scheduled to submit its recommendations to the Florida Legislature before lawmakers convene for their spring session.
